He has not aged is that the years have not passed him by and he has not changed
, according to the language of those who say: He has aged among you, meaning he has lived a year, as the poet said:
x: It is not a year of drought or Rajab, but naked in the years of calamity.

So he made the letter ha’ in the word sunnah the original, which is the classical language. It is not permissible to delete a letter from the Book of God, whether it is stopped or connected, to prove a known aspect in her speech. If a defective person claims that letters have been added to the Qur’an that are extra letters with the intention of stopping, and the original way when reciting is to delete them, such as His statement:
h
Then follow their guidance (al-An’am 6

:90), and His statement: Oh, I wish I had not been given my two books (al-Haqqah 69:25), then this is something about which there is no doubt that it is an extra letter, and that it was added with the intention of stopping. As for what was likely to be the original letter that is not extra, then it is not permissible - and it is confirmed in the Qur’an of the Muslims - to turn it into an extra letter or a connection. However, even if this is an addition to what is undoubtedly an addition, the Arabs may connect a word with an addition and pronounce it in the same way they pronounce it in the case of a break, so their connection to it and their break are the same.

This action of theirs indicates the correctness of the reading of those who read all of this by proving the ha’ in connection and in pause. However, even if this is the case, his sayingل يتسنهhas a ruling that is different from the ruling of what the ha’ is an addition to, there is no doubt about its addition to it.
What indicates the correctness of what we said, that the letter ha in yatasnahu is from the language of those who say: qad asnahat and musanaha, is what:

c: It was narrated to me on the authority of Al-Qasim bin Salam, who said: Ibn Mahdi narrated to us, on the authority of Abu Al-Jarrah, on the authority of Sulayman bin Umair, who said:
m: Hani’, the freed slave of Uthman, narrated to me: I was the messenger between Uthman and Zayd bin Thabit, and Zayd said: Ask him about his saying: It was not made possible or: It was not made possible. Uthman said: Put a ha in it. Al-Qasim narrated, and Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Attar narrated to us, on the authority of al-Qasim, and Ahmad and al-Attar narrated to us, all of them, on the authority of al-Qasim, who said:

c: Ibn Mahdi narrated to us, on the authority of Ibn al-Mubarak,
m: who Surat Al-Baqarah 2:259
h
Or like the one who passed by a town

and it was desolate on its roofs. He said, "How will Allah revive this after its death?" So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then He resurrected him. He said, "How long did you remain?" He said, "I remained a day or part of a day." He said, "Rather, you remained a hundred years. So look at your food and your drink. And look at your donkey, and We will make you a sign to the people. And look at the bones - how We raise them up and then clothe them with flesh. But when it became clear to him, he said, “I know that God has power over all things.” said: Abu Wa’il, a sheikh from the people of Yemen, narrated to me, on the authority of Hani’ al-Barbari, who said: I was with Uthman, and they were showing the copies of the Qur’an, so he sent me with a shoulder of a sheep to Abi ibn Ka’b, in which were written lam yatasnahu and fa-mahal al-kafirin (al-Tariq: 17), and la taddeed li-khalq (al-Rum 30:30). He said: So he called for an inkwell and erased one of the two lams, and wrote la taddeed li-khalq God and erased fa-mahal and wrote fa-mahal al-kafirin and wrote lam yatasnahu and added a ha’ to it.

x: If that had been possible or recommended, Abu would not have added a ha’ to it that has no place in it, nor would Uthman have ordered it to be added to it.

c: It was narrated on the authority of Zaid bin Thabit in this regard,
m: similar to what was narrated on the authority of Abi bin Kaab.
b.via: Zaid bin Thabit in this regard

x: The people of interpretation differed in the interpretation of his saying: He did not make it Sunnah.
Some of them said something similar to what we said, that its meaning is: it did not change.
Who said that?

c: Ibn Hamid told us, he said, Salamah bin al-Mufaddal told us, on the authority of Muhammad bin Ishaq, on the authority of someone
m: who is not accused, on the authority of Wahb bin Munabbih: He did not change it, he did not change it.

c: Bishr told us, he said, Yazid told us, he said, Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada,
m: his saying: He did not change it, did not change.

c: Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us, he said, Abd al-Razzaq told us, he said, Muammar told us, on the authority of Qatada,
m: similarly.

c: Musa bin Harun told me, he said, Amr told us, he said, Asbat told us, on the authority of Al-Suddi:
m: h
Then look at your food and your drink

; it has not become spoiled, meaning: Then look at your food of figs and grapes, and your drink of juice, it has not become spoiled, meaning: it has not changed, so that the figs and grapes have not soured, and the juice has not fermented; they are sweet as they are. That is because he passed by coming from Ash-Sham on his donkey, with juice, grapes, and figs, and God killed him and his donkey, and a hundred years passed over them.

c: It was narrated on the authority of Al-Husayn bin Al-Faraj,
m: who said: I heard Abu Muadh, who said: Ubayd bin Sulayman told us, who said: I heard Al-Dahhak say regarding His statement:
h
Then look at your food and your drink
; it has not become stale, meaning: it has not changed, and a hundred years have passed over it.

c: Al-Muthanna told me, he said, Ishaq told us, he said, Abu Zuhair told us, on the authority of Juwaybir, on the authority of Al-Dahhak,
m: something similar.

c: Al-Muthanna told me, he said, Abdullah told us, he said, Muawiyah told me, on the authority of Ali, on the authority of Ibn Abbas,
m: his saying: He did not change it, did not change.

c: Sufyan told us, he said, my father told us, on the authority of Al-Nadr, on the authority of Ikrimah:
m: He did not change it, he did not change.

c: Yunus told me, he said, Ibn Wahb told us, he said, Ibn Zayd said:
m: It did not change, it did not change in a hundred years.

c: Yunus told me, he said, Ibn Wahb told us, he said, Bakr ibn Mudar told me, he said:
m: They claim in some books that Jeremiah was in Ilia when Nebuchadnezzar destroyed it, so he left it for Egypt, and he was there. Then God revealed to him: Leave it for Jerusalem. So he came to it and found it in ruins. He looked at it and said:
h
How can God revive this after its death

? So God caused him to die for a hundred years, then He resurrected him, and behold, his donkey was alive and standing on its tether, and his food was a basket of grapes and a basket of figs, and it had not changed from its state. Yunus said: Salim al-Khawass told us: His food and drink were a basket of grapes, a basket of figs, and a skin of juice.

x: Others said: The meaning of this is: it did not stink.
Who said that?

c: Muhammad bin Amr told me, he said, Abu Asim told us, on the authority of Isa, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid,
m: regarding his statement: It did not become foul-smelling, it did not smell bad.

c: Al-Muthanna told me, he said, Abu Hudhayfah told us, he said, Shabl told us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid,
m: similarly.

c: Al-Qasim told us, he said, Al-Hasan told us, he said, Hajjaj told me, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, he said,
m: Mujahid said, his statement: to your food, he said: Ask for figs, and your drink, he said: a jug of wine, that has not become stale, he said: has not gone bad.

x: I think that Mujahid, Al-Rabiʿ and those who said the same thing saw that his statement, It did not become foul is from the statement of God Almighty, From altered black mud (al-Hijr 15:26, 28, 33), meaning the smell of which changes with stench, from the statement of the speaker: It became foul. The evidence has been explained previously that this is not the case. If someone thought that it was from the old ones, from the saying of the speaker: This water has become old, it has become old, as God Almighty said:
In it are rivers of water that is not putrid

then if that were the case, the statement would be: So look at your food and drink, it has not become putrid, and it has not become putrid. [If it is said]: It is from him, except that he left out the hamza. It was said: Even if he left out the hamza, it is not permissible to double the nun, because the nun is not doubled, and it is doubled in yatasanna.

If the one who says yatasanna left out the hamza, it would be said: yatasanna with a light nun without a ha’ added to it. In that is a clear statement that it is not permissible for it to be from asn.
The people of interpretation differed in their interpretation of His statement: And look at your donkey.

Some of them said: The meaning of this is: And look at My bringing your donkey back to life, and at its bones, how I raised them up and then covered them with flesh. Then the interpreters of this differed in their interpretation.

Some of them said: God Almighty said that to him, after He had revived him as a sound creation, then He wanted to revive his donkey, as a way for Him Almighty to explain to him how He revived the village that he saw as desolate, so he said:
h
How can God revive this after its death
? denouncing God’s revival of it.

Who said that? Ibn Humayd narrated, Salamah narrated, on the authority of Ibn Ishaq, on the authority of someone who is not accused, on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih, who said: God sent him and said: How long did you remain? He said: A day or part of a day until His saying: Then We covered it with flesh. He said: So he looked at his donkey, some parts connected to others, and it had died with him, with the veins and nerves, then He covered it with flesh from it until it was even, then the soul ran through it and it stood up braying. He looked at its juice and softness, and behold, it was as it was when he was born, it had not changed. So when he saw what he saw of God’s power, he said: I know that God has power over all things.

c: Musa told me, Amr told us, Asbat told us, on the authority of Al-Suddi:
m: Then God revived Ezra and said: How long have you remained? He said: I have remained for a day or part of a day! He said: Rather, you have remained for a hundred years! Look at your food and drink, they have not stale, and look at your donkey, it has perished and its bones have decayed, and look at its bones, how We raise them up and then cover them with flesh. Then God sent a wind that brought the bones of the donkey from every plain and mountain, which the birds and beasts had taken away, and they gathered together, and some of them mounted on others while he was watching, and it became a donkey of bones, without flesh or blood. Then God covered the bones with flesh and blood, and it became a donkey of flesh and blood, but without a soul in it. Then an angel came walking and took hold of the donkey’s nostril and blew into it, and the donkey brayed, I know that God has power over all things.

x: The interpretation of the statement is as the speaker of this statement interpreted it: And look at our bringing your donkey back to life, and at his bones - how We raise them up and then clothe them with flesh, and that We may make you a sign for the people. So in his statement: And look at your donkey, there is something omitted from the statement that is sufficient in its apparent meaning from mentioning it, and the alif and lam in his statement:
h
And look at the bones are a substitute for the ha’ intended in the
meaning, because its meaning is: And look at his bones - meaning: at the bones of the donkey.

Others among them said: Rather, God Almighty said that to him after He breathed the spirit into his eye. They said: It was the first of His limbs into which He breathed the spirit, and that was after He created him in a perfect form, and before He revived his donkey.
Who said that?

c: Muhammad bin Amr told me, he said, Abu Asim told us, he said, Isa told us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, he said:
m: This was a man from the Children of Israel into whose eyes the spirit was breathed, so he looked at all of his creation when God brought him back to life, and at his donkey when God brought him back to life.

c: Al-Muthanna told me, he said, Abu Hudhayfah told us, he said, Shabl told us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid,
m: similarly.

c: Al-Qasim narrated to us, Al-Husayn narrated to us, Hajjaj narrated to me, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, who said:
m: He began with his eyes and breathed life into them, then with his bones and raised them up, then joined some of them to others, then covered them with nerves, then veins, then bones come together, for God has sent down a spirit upon you. So each bone ran to its companion, and he joined the bones, then the nerves, then the veins, then the flesh, then the skin, then the hair. His donkey was a trunk, but He revived it as an adult, and it had become unkempt from the passage of time, and nothing remained of it except the skin. His food was a basket of grapes, and his drink was a jug of wine. Ibn Jurayj said on the authority of Mujahid: He breathed life into his eyes, then looked with them at all of His creation when God resurrected it, and at his donkey when God revived it.

x: Others said: Rather, God placed the soul in his head and his sight, and his body was dead. So he saw his donkey standing as it was on the day he tied it up, and his food and drink as it was on the day he arrived at the spot. Then God said to him: Look at the bones of your soul, how We will resurrect them. Mention who told you: Muhammad bin Sahl bin Askar told me, he said, Ismail bin Abdul Karim told us, he said, Abdul Samad bin Surat Al-Baqarah 2:259
h
Or like the one who passed by a town

and it was desolate on its roofs. He said, "How will Allah revive this after its death?" So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then He resurrected him. He said, "How long did you remain?" He said, "I remained a day or part of a day." He said, "Rather, you remained a hundred years. So look at your food and your drink. And look at your donkey, and We will make you a sign to the people. And look at the bones - how We raise them up and then clothe them with flesh.
But when it became clear to him, he said, “I know that God has power over all things.”

c: Maqal told me:
m: He heard Wahb bin Munabbih say: God restored the spirit of life to the eye of Jeremiah, and the end of his body was dead. He looked at his food and drink, and they did not stagnate. He looked at his donkey standing as it was on the day he tied it up, it did not eat or drink. He looked at the ashes on the donkey’s neck, and they did not change, they were new.

c: It was narrated on the authority of Al-Husayn,
m: who said: I heard Abu Muadh, who said: Ubayd ibn Sulayman narrated to us, who said: I heard Ad-Dahhak say regarding His statement:
h
Then God caused him to die for a hundred years

, then He resurrected him. He looked at his donkey standing, having remained for a hundred years, and at his food, which had not changed, having been for a hundred years. And look at the bones, how We raise them up and then cover them with flesh. The first thing that God revived from it was its head, and then he began to look at the rest of His creation being created.

c: Al-Muthanna told me, he said, Ishaq told us, he said, Abu Zuhair told us, on the authority of Juwaybir, on the authority of Al-Dahhak,
m: regarding his statement:
h
Then God caused him to die for a hundred years and then resurrected him

, he looked at his donkey standing, and at his food and drink, and they had not changed. The first thing that was created from it was its head, so he began to look at every part of it, connecting some of it to others. When it became clear to him, he said: I know that God is over all things competent.

c: Bishr bin Muadh told us, Yazid told us, Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada, who said:
m: It was mentioned to us that the first thing God created from him was his head, then his eyes were placed in him, then it was said to him: Look! So he began to look, and his bones began to connect with each other, and that happened through the eyes of the Prophet of God, peace be upon him, and he said: I know that God is capable of all things.

c: It was narrated on the authority of Ammar,
m: who said: Ibn Abi Jaʿfar narrated to us, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ar-Rabiʿ: Then look at your food and drink, they have not become spoiled, and look at your donkey, and his donkey was with him as it was,
h
And We will make you a sign for the people

, “And look at the bones, how We raise them up.” Ar-Rabiʿ said: It was mentioned to us, and God knows best, that the first thing created from him was his eyes, then it was said: Look! So he began to look at the bones, some of them connected to each other, and that was with his eyes, and he said: I know that God has power over all things.

c: Yunus told me, he said, Ibn Wahb told us, he said, Ibn Zayd told us, he said:
m: His statement, “
h
Then look at your food and your drink

, it has not spoiled. And look at your donkey,” standing over you for a hundred years, “and that We may make you a sign to mankind. And look at the bones,” he said: And look at your bones, how We bring them to life when you asked Us: How do We bring these to life? He said: So God put the spirit in his sight and in his tongue, then He said: Call now with your tongue, in which God put the spirit, and look with your sight. He said: So he was looking at the skull. He said: So he called: Let every bone join its friend. He said: So every bone came to its companion, until it connected while he was watching it, until a piece of bone would come to the place from which it was broken and stick to it, until it reached his skull while he was watching that. So when it connected, He strengthened it with nerves and veins and filled it with flesh and skin, then He breathed the spirit into it, then He said: And look at the bones, how We raise them up and then cover them with flesh. When that became clear to him, he said: I know that God is capable of all things. He said: Then he ordered that those bones be called out, about which he said:
h
How can God revive these after their death
? just as he had called out to his own bones, then God revived them just as He revived him.

c: Yunus told me, he said, Ibn Wahb told us, he said, Bakr ibn Mudar told me, he said:
m: They claim in some books: God caused Jeremiah to die for a hundred years, then resurrected him, and behold, his donkey was alive and standing on its tether. He said: God restored his sight to him, and put the spirit in him thirty years before he was resurrected, then he looked at Jerusalem and how it was inhabited and what was around it. He said: They say, and God knows best, that he is the one about whom God Almighty said: Or like one who passed by a town and it was desolate, the verse. The meaning of the verse according to their interpretation is: Look at your donkey,
h
and We will make you a sign for the people

. Look at your bones, how We will raise them up after their decay, then clothe them with flesh and give them life through your life. So learn how God gives life to the towns and their people after their death.

x: The most correct of the sayings about this verse is the saying of the one who said: God, the Most High, sent someone who said:
h
How can God revive this after its death

? from his own death, then showed him something similar to what he found strange about God reviving the village he passed by after its death, clearly from himself, his food, and his donkey. So God, the Most High, made what he saw of his reviving himself and his donkey an example of what he found strange about his reviving the people of the village he passed by, which was empty and empty of its roofs, and made what he saw of the lesson in his food and drink a lesson for him and an argument against him about how he revived the houses and gardens of the village. And that is the meaning of the saying of Mujahid that we mentioned before. Rather, we said: This is more appropriate for the interpretation of the verse because His statement: And look at the bones, means: And look at the bones that you see with your eyes, how We raise them up and then cover them with flesh.

And his donkey had become worn out, according to all the people of interpretation, similar to what happened to the bones of the one addressed with this speech. So it is not possible to divert the meaning of His statement: And look at the bones, to him being commanded to look at the bones of the donkey rather than the bones of the one he was commanded to look at, nor to him being commanded to look at his own bones rather than the bones of the donkey. Since that was the case, and the wear and tear had affected his bones and the bones of his donkey, it would have been more appropriate for the interpretation to be that the command be to look at everything that his eye could see of what had become worn out. Because God, the Most High, made all of that an argument against him, and a lesson and admonition for him.
God Almighty means by that:
h
And We will make you a sign for the people
. We kept you alive for a hundred years, then We resurrected you. The waw was inserted with the lam in His statement:
h
And We will make you a sign for the people

, which means so that, because its inclusion in ki and its sisters indicates that it is a condition for the action that comes after it, meaning: And We will make you such and such, We did that. If there was no waw before the lam - I mean the lam of ki - the lam would have been a condition for the action that came before it, and its meaning would have been: And look at your donkey, We will make you a sign for the people. What he meant by his saying: And We will make you a sign, is that We will make you an argument against those who are ignorant of My power and doubt My greatness. I am able to do whatever I will of causing death and giving life, annihilation and creation, bestowing favors and humiliating, poverty and enrichment.
All of that is in My hand. No one possesses it except Me, and no one is able to do it except Me.
Some of the interpreters said: He was a sign for the people, because he came after a hundred years to his son and his son’s son, a young man while they were old.
Who said that?

c: Al-Muthanna told me, he said, Ishaq told us, he said, Qubaysah bin Uqbah told us, on the authority of Sufyan, he said:
m: I heard Al-A’mash say: And We will make you a sign to the people. He said: A young man and his children were old men.

x: Others said: The meaning of that is: He came and those who knew him had perished, so he was a sign to those of his people who came to him.
Who said that?

c: Musa told me, he said, Amr told us, he said, Asbat told us, on the authority of Al-Suddi, he said:
m: He returned to his family and found that his house had been sold and rebuilt, and that those he knew had perished. He said: Get out of my house! They said: Who are you? He said: I am Ezra! They said: Didn’t Ezra perish such and such a time ago? He said: I am Ezra, he was like me and he was! So when they knew that, they got out of the house and gave it to him.

x: What is more appropriate for the interpretation of the verse than the statement is to say: God Almighty mentioned that He made the one whose description was described in this verse an argument for the people, so that was an argument against those of his children and his people who knew him, who knew of his death and God’s revival of him after his death, and against those of them to whom He was sent.

We have previously demonstrated that the bones that he was commanded to look at were the bones of himself and his donkey, and we mentioned the differences of opinion among those who differed in interpreting that, and what each speaker meant by what he said in that, so there is no need to repeat it. As for his saying: How do we raise it up?, the readings differed in its reading.

Some of them read it as: And look at the bones, how We bring them together, with a damma on the nun and a zay. This is the general reading of the Kufians, meaning: And look how We put some of them on top of others, and transfer that to places in the body. The root of the word nashuz is to rise. It is said, The boy has become nashuz, if he has grown tall and matured. It is also said, The woman is nashuz with her husband. It is also said, The high place on the ground is called nashuz, nashuz, and nashaz. If you mean that you raised it, you say, I raised it inshazan, and nashuz hu, if it rose. The meaning of his saying: And look at the bones, how We raise them up - according to the reading of those who read it with a zay - is how We raise them from their places in the earth, and return them to their places in the body. Among those who interpreted this interpretation were a group of people of interpretation.
Who said that?

c: Al-Muthanna told me, he said, Abdullah bin Saleh told us, he said, Muawiyah told me, on the authority of Ali, on the authority of Ibn Abbas,
m: regarding his statement: How do We raise it up? How do We bring it out?

c: Musa told me, he said, Amr told us, he said, Asbat told us, on the authority of Al-Suddi:
m: How do we raise it? He said: We move it.

x: Others read it as: And look at the bones, how We resurrect them with a damma on the nun. They said: It is from the saying of the speaker, God resurrects the dead, so He resurrects them, and this is how the majority of the people of Medina read it, meaning: And look at the bones, how We bring them to life, then Surat Al-Baqarah 2:259
h
Or like the one who passed by a town

and it was desolate on its roofs. He said, "How will Allah revive this after its death?" So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then He resurrected him. He said, "How long did you remain?" He said, "I remained a day or part of a day." He said, "Rather, you remained a hundred years. So look at your food and your drink. And look at your donkey, and We will make you a sign to the people. And look at the bones - how We raise them up and then clothe them with flesh. But when it became clear to him, he said, “I know that God has power over all things.” clothe them with flesh.
Who said that?

c: Muhammad bin Amr told me, he said, Abu Asim told us, he said, Isa told us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid:
m: How do we resurrect it? He said: Look at it when God resurrects it.

c: Al-Muthanna told me, he said, Abu Hudhayfah told us, he said, Shabl told us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid,
m: similarly.

c: Bishr told us, he said, Yazid told us, he said, Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada,
m: similarly.

c: Yunus told me, he said, Ibn Wahb told us, he said, Ibn Zayd said
m: regarding His statement, And look at the bones, how We resurrect them, he said: How We bring them to life.

x: Some of the reciters of this verse cited the letter ra and the damma of the letter nun at the beginning, in his saying: Then if He wills, He will resurrect him
r
(Abasa 80:22)
, so he saw that it was correct to add to his saying: And look at the bones, how We resurrect them thereby.

Some of them read it as: And look at the bones, how We spread them out, with the opening of the letter noon at the beginning and with the letter ra. It is as if he directed that to something similar in meaning: spreading something out and folding it. This is an undesirable reading, because the Arabs do not say: spreading the dead, but rather they say: God raised the dead, so they were raised, meaning He revived them, so they were revived. This is indicated by His statement: Then when He wills, He will raise him up and His statement: Or have they taken gods from the earth who will raise them up?
r
(Al-Anbiya’: 21)

. And that if it is meant by it that the dead person is brought to life and lives after his death, it is said: spreading, and from this is the statement of A’sha of Banu Tha’labah: Until people say from what they saw: Oh, how strange is the dead one who spreads!

c: It was narrated by hearing from the Arabs:
m: He had scabies and it spread, if his skin returned.

x: My opinion on this matter is that the meaning of inshaz and inshar are close. Because the meaning of inshaz is composition and establishment and returning bones to bones, and the meaning of inshar is restoring life to bones. Restoring them is undoubtedly returning them to their places and locations in the body after they have left it. So, even though they differ in wording, they are close in meaning. The nation has come to recite them in a way that eliminates excuses and requires proof. So whichever one the reader recites is correct, because their meanings are subservient, and there is no proof that requires one of them to be judged as correct over the other. If someone thinks that resurrection is revival, then he is more correct, because the one who was commanded to look at the bones being resurrected was only commanded to do so in order to see with his own eyes what he denied by saying: How will God revive these after their death? [He has made a mistake].

For there is no doubt that reviving the bones in this place means returning them to their places in the body of the one being looked at, which is He who is revived, in order to restore the soul that had left them at death. What indicates this is His saying: Then We covered them with flesh. There is no doubt that the soul was only breathed into the bones that were resurrected after they had been covered with flesh. Since this is the case, and the meaning of reconstruction is the assembly of bones and their return to their places in the body, and this is the meaning of spreading, it is known that their two meanings are equal, and that they agree in meaning and do not differ. In that is a clarification of the correctness of what we have said about it. As for the third reading, I do not consider it permissible to read it. It is the reading of those who read: How shall we spread it with the opening of the letter nun and the letter ra, because it is an anomaly of the reading of Muslims and its departure from the correct and eloquent speech of the Arabs.

God Almighty meant by His statement: Then We covered them with flesh, meaning the bones, “and the ha’ in His statement: “Then We covered them with flesh,” is from the mention of the bones. The meaning of naksooha is that we dress it and cover it with it, just as a person’s body is covered by the clothing he wears. The Arabs do the same, they make everything that covers something and conceals it, a garment and cover for it. From this is the saying of Al-Nabigha Al-Ja’di: Praise be to God that my death did not come until I had put on a garment of Islam. So Islam - by covering what he was wearing, concealing it and eliminating it - made it his clothing and garment.

God Almighty means by His statement: So when it became clear to him, when it became clear to him clearly what he had found strange about God’s power and greatness before he had seen it, he said, ‘I know,’ now after seeing it, clarifying it, and explaining it, ‘that God has power over all things.’ Then the reading differed in the reading of his saying: He said, ‘I know that God…’ Some of them read it: He said, know meaning a command to connect the alif of I know, and to make the meem jazm from it, and this is a general reading of the people of Kufa. They mention that in the reading of Abdullah, It was said, know is a command from God who gave life after his death, so he was commanded to look at what God will give life to after his death. And this is also narrated from Ibn Abbas.

c: Ahmad bin Yusuf al-Taghlabi told me, he said, al-Qasim bin Salam told us, he said, Hajjaj told me, on the authority of Harun, he said:
m: It is in Abdullah’s reading: It was said, know that God in the form of a command.

c: Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us, he said, Abd al-Razzaq told us, he said, Muammar told us, on the authority of Ibn Tawus, on the authority of his father - I think it was him,
m: Abu Jaʿfar al-Tabari was not sure - I heard Ibn Abbas recite: And when it became clear to him, he said, Know. He said: That was only said to him.
b.via: his father - I think it was him

c: It was narrated on the authority of Ammar,
m: who said: Ibn Abi Jaʿfar narrated to us, on the authority of his father, on the authority of al-Rabiʿ, who said: It was mentioned to us, and God knows best, that it was said to him: Look! So he began to look at the bones, how some of them were connected to others, and that was with his eyes, and it was said: Know that God is capable of all things.

x: According to this statement, the interpretation of that is: When what was made clear to him of God’s command and power became clear to him, God said to him: Know now that God has power over all things. If the interpreter of his statement: He said, know - and he read it as a command - were to refer it to the one about whom he was informed of what was related in this verse of his story, it would be a correct interpretation, and that would be like the speaker saying: Know that such and such happened, as a command from him to someone else, and he means himself by it.

Others read it as: He said, I know, as a report about himself to the speaker, with a hamza on the alif of I know and its severing, and raising the mim, meaning: So when what became clear to him of God’s power and great authority became clear through his witnessing what he witnessed, he said: The one who made that clear: I know now that God is capable of everything. This is how most of the people of Medina read it, and some of the people of Iraq read it. This is how a group of people of interpretation interpreted it.
Who said that?

c: Ibn Hamid told us, he said, Salamah told us, on the authority of Ibn Ishaq, on the authority of someone
m: who is not accused, on the authority of Wahb ibn Munabbih, he said: When he witnessed what he witnessed of God’s power, he said: I know that God is capable of everything.

c: Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us, he said: Abd al-Razzaq told us, he said: Abd al-Samad bin Muqal told us:
m: that he heard Wahb Munabbih say: “When it became clear to him, he said: I know that God is capable of all things.”

c: Bishr told us, he said, Yazid told us, he said, Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada, he said:
m: With the eye of the Prophet of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, meaning the resurrection of the bones, then he said: I know that God is capable of everything.

c: Musa told me, he said, Amr told us, he said, Asbat told us, on the authority of Al-Suddi, he said:
m: Uzair said at that time - meaning when he witnessed God reviving his donkey - I know that God is capable of all things.

c: Al-Muthanna told me, he said, Ishaq told us, he said, Abu Zuhair told us, on the authority of Juwaybir, on the authority of Al-Dahhak, he said:
m: He began to look at every part of it, connecting some of it to others, and when it became clear to him, he said, ‘I know that God is over all things competent.’

c: Yunus told me, he said, Ibn Wahb told us, he said,
m: Ibn Zayd said something similar.

x: The more correct of the two readings in this regard is the reading of the one who reads: Know by connecting the alif and making the mim jazm, as a command from God, the Most High, to the one who brought him back to life after his death, by commanding him to know that God - who showed him with his own eyes what he saw of His great power and authority, by bringing him and his donkey back to life after a hundred years of death and affliction, until they returned to the state they were in on the day He took their souls, and preserved his food and drink for him for a hundred years until He returned him to him in the state he was in on the day he placed him, unchanged - is capable of everything in this way. We chose to read it in this way, and judged it to be correct, rather than anything else, because what preceded it of speech was a command from God Almighty: a statement to the one whom God revived after his death, and an address to him with it, and that is His saying:
h
Then look at your food and your drink
, it has not spoiled, and look at your donkey… And look at the bones, how We raise them up.
So when that became clear to him in response to his question to his Lord:
h
How can God revive these after their death

? God said to him: Know that God, who did these things as you saw, is capable of other things, just as He is capable of what you saw and the like, as God Almighty said to His friend Abraham, peace be upon him, after He answered his question to Him in His saying: My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead, “And know that God is Exalted in Might and Wise.” So He commanded Abraham to know, after He showed him how He revives the dead, that He is Exalted in Might and Wise. So likewise was the command of the one who asked, saying: How can God give life to these after their death? After I showed him how to revive it, he should know that God is capable of everything. Surat Al-Baqarah 2:259
h
Or like the one who passed by a town
and it was desolate on its roofs. He said, "How will Allah revive this after its death?"

So Allah caused him to die for a hundred years, then He resurrected him. He said, "How long did you remain?" He said, "I remained a day or part of a day." He said, "Rather, you remained a hundred years. So look at your food and your drink. And look at your donkey, and We will make you a sign to the people. And look at the bones - how We raise them up and then clothe them with flesh. But when it became clear to him, he said, “I know that God has power over all things.”

evidence.text: And whoever reads it like that, then he makes the ha’ in yatasanna an extra conjunction, like his saying: So follow their guidance (al-An’am 6:90), and he made tafa’alat from it: tasnayt tasnayyan, and he reasoned in that by saying that sunnah is the plural of sanawat, so tafa’alat is correct.
It is a general reading of the Kufa reading.

Whoever reads it in this way, then he makes the ha’ in yatasanna the lam of the verb, and makes it jussive with lam, and makes fa’ala from it: tasannahat and yaf’ulu atsanah tasannahan, and he said in the diminutive of sunnah sanayha and suniyah, asnayt ‘ad’l-qawm and asnahat ‘ad’l-hum, if you stayed for a year.
This is a general reading of the people of Medina and Hijaz.

Abu Jaafar said: The correct reading in my opinion is to prove the ha’ in both connected and paused pronunciations, because it is proven in the Muslims’ Mushaf, and there is a correct explanation for proving it in both cases.
This action of theirs indicates the correctness of the reading of those who read all of this by proving the ha’ in connection and in pause.
As for his saying: How do we raise it up?, the readings differed in its reading.
Some of them read it as: And look at the bones, how We bring them together, with a damma on the nun and a zay.
This is the general reading of the Kufians, meaning: And look how We put some of them on top of others, and transfer that to places in the body.

The meaning of his saying: And look at the bones, how We raise them up - according to the reading of those who read it with a zay - is how We raise them from their places in the earth, and return them to their places in the body.
Others read it as: And look at the bones, how We resurrect them with a damma on the nun.

They said: It is from the saying of the speaker, God resurrects the dead, so He resurrects them, and this is how the majority of the people of Medina read it, meaning: And look at the bones, how We bring them to life, then Surat Al-Baqarah 2:259 Or like the one who passed by a town and it was desolate on its roofs.

Some of the reciters of this verse cited the letter ra and the damma of the letter nun at the beginning, in his saying: Then if He wills, He will resurrect him (Abasa 80:22), so he saw that it was correct to add to his saying: And look at the bones, how We resurrect them thereby.
Some of them read it as: And look at the bones, how We spread them out, with the opening of the letter noon at the beginning and with the letter ra.
The nation has come to recite them in a way that eliminates excuses and requires proof.
As for the third reading, I do not consider it permissible to read it.

It is the reading of those who read: How shall we spread it with the opening of the letter nun and the letter ra, because it is an anomaly of the reading of Muslims and its departure from the correct and eloquent speech of the Arabs.

Then the reading differed in the reading of his saying: He said, ‘I know that God…’ Some of them read it: He said, know meaning a command to connect the alif of I know, and to make the meem jazm from it, and this is a general reading of the people of Kufa.
They mention that in the reading of Abdullah, It was said, know is a command from God who gave life after his death, so he was commanded to look at what God will give life to after his death.

If the interpreter of his statement: He said, know - and he read it as a command - were to refer it to the one about whom he was informed of what was related in this verse of his story, it would be a correct interpretation, and that would be like the speaker saying: Know that such and such happened, as a command from him to someone else, and he means himself by it.

Others read it as: He said, I know, as a report about himself to the speaker, with a hamza on the alif of I know and its severing, and raising the mim, meaning: So when what became clear to him of God’s power and great authority became clear through his witnessing what he witnessed, he said: The one who made that clear: I know now that God is capable of everything.
This is how most of the people of Medina read it, and some of the people of Iraq read it.

Abu Jaʿfar said: The more correct of the two readings in this regard is the reading of the one who reads: Know by connecting the alif and making the mim jazm, as a command from God, the Most High, to the one who brought him back to life after his death, by commanding him to know that God - who showed him with his own eyes what he saw of His great power and authority, by bringing him and his donkey back to life after a hundred years of death and affliction, until they returned to the state they were in on the day He took their souls, and preserved his food and drink for him for a hundred years until He returned him to him in the state he was in on the day he placed him, unchanged - is capable of everything in this way.

We chose to read it in this way, and judged it to be correct, rather than anything else, because what preceded it of speech was a command from God Almighty: a statement to the one whom God revived after his death, and an address to him with it, and that is His saying: Then look at your food and your drink, it has not spoiled, and look at your donkey… And look at the bones, how We raise them up.

x: God Almighty means by that: Did you not see when Abraham said: My Lord, show me. It is appropriate to connect the words
h
And when Abraham said

to the words Or like the one who passed by a town, and the words Have you not seen the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord? because the words Have you not seen do not mean Have you not seen with your eyes, but rather the meaning is Have you not seen with your heart, so its meaning is Have you not known and remembered? Even though its wording is the wording of seeing, it is sometimes connected to it with words that agree with its wording, and sometimes with words that agree with its meaning.
The interpreters differed about the reason for Abraham’s question to his Lord to show him how He revives death.

Some of them said: His question to his Lord was that he saw a beast that had been divided into beasts and birds, so he asked his Lord to show him how He revived it, with its flesh being dispersed in the bellies of birds of the air and beasts of the earth, so that he could see that with his own eyes, and his certainty would increase by seeing it with his own eyes, to his knowledge of it, so God showed him that as an example of what He had informed him that He had commanded him to do.
Who said that?

c: Bishr bin Muadh told us, Yazid bin Zari’ told us, Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada,
m: regarding his statement:
h
And when Abraham said

, ‘My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead,’ He mentioned to us that the friend of God, Abraham, came upon a beast that was scattered among beasts and wild animals, and he said: My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead. He said, Do you not believe? He said, Yes, but
h
so that my heart may be reassured

c: It was narrated on the authority of Al-Husayn,
m: who said: I heard Abu Muadh, who said: Ubayd told us, who said: I heard Ad-Dahhak say about His statement: My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead. He said: Ibrahim passed by a dead animal that had decayed and had been torn apart by the winds and wild beasts. He stood looking and said: Glory be to God! How does God give life to this? And he knew that God was able to do that. So that is what He said: My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.

c: Al-Qasim narrated to us, Al-Husayn narrated to us, Hajjaj narrated to me, Ibn Jurayj said:
m: It reached me that while Ibrahim was walking on the road, he came upon the carcass of a donkey with wild beasts and birds on it. Its flesh had been torn apart, leaving only its bones. When the wild beasts had gone and the birds had flown to the mountains and hills, he stopped and marveled, then said: My Lord, I know that you will gather them from the bellies of these wild beasts and birds! My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead! He said: Do you not believe? He said: Yes! But hearing is not like seeing it in person.

c: Yunus told me, he said, Ibn Wahb told us, he said, Ibn Zayd said:
m: Abraham passed by a fish, half of which was on land and half of it was in the sea. That part of it was in the sea, eaten by the creatures of the sea, and that part of it was on land, eaten by the wild beasts and creatures of the land. The wicked one said to him: O Abraham, when will God gather this from the bellies of these? He said: O Lord, show me how You give life to the dead! He said: Do you not believe? He said: Yes! But
h
so that my heart may be reassured

x: Others said: Rather, the reason for his asking his Lord for that was the debate and argument that took place between him and Nimrod about that.
Who said that?

c: Ibn Humayd told us, Salamah told us, Muhammad ibn Ishaq told me:
m: When what happened between Abraham and his people happened, as God related in Surat al-Anbiya, Nimrod said, regarding what they mentioned, to Abraham: Have you seen this god of yours, whom you worship and call others to worship, and whose power you mention that you glorify over others, what is it? Abraham said to him: My Lord is He who gives life and causes death! Nimrod said: I give life and cause death! Abraham said to him: How do you give life and cause death? Then he mentioned what God related of his argument with him. He said: Abraham said at that time: My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead. He said: Do you not believe? He said: Yes, but
h
so that my heart may be reassured
, Surat Al-Baqarah 2:260
h
And when Abraham said

, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." He said, "Do you not believe?" He said, "Yes, but [it is] to reassure my heart." He said, "Then take four birds and bring them close to you, then place a portion of them on every mountain, then call them, they will come to you running. And know that God is Exalted in Might and Wise." without doubt in God, the Most High, nor in His power, but he wanted to know that and his heart longed for it, so he said:
h
So that my heart may be reassured
, meaning: what it longed for if he knew it.

x: These two statements - I mean the first and the second - are close in meaning: that Abraham’s question to his Lord to show him how He revives the dead was so that he could see with his own eyes what he had of knowledge of that.

Others said: Rather, his question to his Lord was that he received the good report from God that He had chosen him as a friend, so he asked his Lord to show him an immediate sign of that, so that his heart would be reassured that He had chosen him as a friend for Himself, and that would be supported by the certainty he had.
Who said that?

c: Musa bin Harun told me, Amr told us, Asbat told us, on the authority of Al-Suddi, who said:
m: When God chose Abraham as a friend, the Angel of Death asked his Lord to permit him to give Abraham the good report of that, and He gave him permission. So he came to Abraham who was not at home, so he entered his house, and Abraham was the most jealous of people. If he went out, he would close the door. When he came and found a man in his house, he rushed to him to seize him and said: Who gave you permission to enter my house? The Angel of Death said: The Lord of this house gave me permission! Abraham said: You are right! And he knew that he was the Angel of Death. He said: Who are you? He said: I am the Angel of Death, I have come to give you the good report that God has chosen you as a friend! So he praised God and said: O Angel of Death, show me the image in which you take the breaths of the infidels. He said: O Abraham, you cannot bear that! He said: Yes! He said: Then turn away! So Abraham turned away and looked at him, and behold, he was a black man whose head reached the sky, and flames of fire were coming out of his mouth. There was not a hair on his body except that he was in the form of a black man from whose mouth and ears flames of fire were coming out. Then Ibrahim fainted, then he came to and the Angel of Death had transformed into the first image. He said: O Angel of Death, if the unbeliever faced nothing at the time of death from affliction and sorrow except your image, that would suffice him. So show me how You take the breaths of the believers? He said: Turn away! So Ibrahim turned away, then he turned and saw a young man, the most handsome of people in face and the sweetest of scents, wearing white clothes. He said: O Angel of Death, if the believer had nothing from the comfort of his eye and honor with his Lord except this image of yours, it would suffice him. So the Angel of Death departed, and Ibrahim stood up, supplicating to his Lord, saying: O Lord, show me how You give life to the dead so that I may know that I am Your intimate friend! He said: Do you not believe that I am Your intimate friend? - He said: Believe - He said: Yes! But
h
so that my heart may be reassured
by Your intimate friend.

c: Ahmad bin Ishaq told us, Abu Ahmad Al-Zubayri told us, Amr bin Thabit told us, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubair:
m: But
h
so that my heart may be reassured
, he said: with friendship.

x: Others said: He said that to his Lord because he doubted God’s ability to revive the dead.
Who said that?

c: Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us, he said, Abd al-Razzaq told us, he said, Muammar told us, on the authority of Ayoub,
m: regarding his statement:
h
But that my heart may be reassured

, he said: Ibn Abbas said: There is no verse in the Qur’an that I hope for more than it. Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated, Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar narrated, Shuʿbah narrated, I heard Zayd ibn ʿAli narrating on the authority of a man, on the authority of Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, who said: ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbbas and ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr promised to meet - and we were young at that time - and one of them said to the other: Which verse in the Book of God has the greatest hope for this nation? ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr said: “Say: O My servants who have transgressed against themselves” (al-Zumar 39:53), until he finished the verse. Ibn ʿAbbas said: As for you saying: It is - and what is more hopeful for this nation than it is the saying of Abraham, peace be upon him: My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead. He said: Do you not believe? He said: Yes, but
h
so that my heart may be reassured

c: Al-Qasim told us, Al-Husayn told us, Hajjaj told me, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, who said:
m: I asked Ata’ bin Abi Rabah about His statement:
h
And when Abraham said

, ‘My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.’ He said, ‘Do you not believe?’ He said, ‘Yes, but [to] reassure my heart.’ He said that something entered Abraham’s heart that enters people’s hearts, so he said, My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead. He said, Do you not believe? He said, Yes. He said, Then take four birds, to show him.

c: Zakariya bin Yahya bin Aban Al-Masry told me, he said: Saeed bin Talid told us, he said: Abd Al-Rahman bin Al-Qasim told us, he said: Bakr bin Mudar told me, on the authority of Amr bin Al-Harith, on the authority of Yunus bin Yazid, on the authority of Ibn Shihab, he said: Abu Salamah bin Abd Al-Rahman and Saeed bin Al-Musayyab told me, on the authority of Abu Hurairah,
m: “The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said:
h
We are more deserving of doubt than Abraham
. He said: ‘My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead.’ He said: ‘Do you not believe?’ He said: ‘Yes, but
h
so that my heart may be reassured

c: Yunus told me, he said, Ibn Wahb told us, he said, Yunus told me, on the authority of Ibn Shihab and Saeed bin Al-Musayyab, on the authority of Abu Hurairah,
m: that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said, and he mentioned something similar.

x: The most correct of these sayings in interpreting the verse is what is authentically reported from the Messenger of God (may God bless him and grant him peace) that he said, which is his saying:
h
We are more deserving of doubt than Abraham

. He said: My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead! He said: Do you not believe? And that his question to his Lord was that he asked Him to show him how to give life to the dead because of an impediment from Satan that appeared in his heart, like what we mentioned from Ibn Zayd earlier: that when Abraham saw the whale, part of which was on land and part of which was in the sea, and the beasts of the land and the beasts of the sea and the birds of the air, Satan cast a spell into his soul and he said: When will God gather this from the bellies of these? So Abraham then asked his Lord to show him how He gives life to the dead, so that he could witness it with his own eyes, and after that Satan would not be able to cast into his heart the same as he cast into it when he saw what he saw of that.

So his Lord said to him: Do you not believe? He said: Did you not believe, O Abraham, that I am able to do that? He said: Yes, O Lord! But I asked you to show me that so that my heart would be reassured, and that Satan would not be able to put into my heart what he did when I saw this whale.

c: Yunus told me that, he said, Ibn Wahb told us, on the authority of Ibn Zayd.
m: The meaning of his saying:
h
So that my heart may be reassured is so that it may be calmed and at peace with the certainty that it has
. This interpretation that we have mentioned about that is the interpretation of those who directed the meaning of his saying:
h
So that my heart may be reassured to
: so that faith may increase, or: so that he may be certain. He mentioned that he said: to be certain, or: to increase certainty or faith.

c: Abu Kuraib told us, he said, Abu Naim told us, on the authority of Sufyan, on the authority of Qais bin Muslim, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubair:
m: h
So that my heart may be reassured
, he said: So that it may be certain.

c: Muhammad bin Bashar told us, he said, Abd al-Rahman told us, he said, Sufyan told us, and Ahmad bin Ishaq told us, he said, Abu Ahmad told us, he said, Sufyan told us, on the authority of Abu al-Haytham, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubayr:
m: h
So that my heart may be reassured
, he said: So that my certainty may increase.

c: Al-Muthanna told me, he said, Ishaq told us, he said, Abu Zuhair told us, on the authority of Juwaybir, on the authority of Al-Dahhak:
m: But
h
so that my heart may be reassured
, he said: so that my certainty may increase.

c: Bishr bin Muadh told us, he said, Yazid told us, he said, Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada:
m: But
h
so that my heart may be reassured
. He said: And the Prophet of God, Abraham, wanted to increase his certainty to his certainty.

c: Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us, he said, Abd al-Razzaq told us, he said,
m: Muammar said, Qatada said: To increase his certainty.

c: It was narrated on the authority of Ammar,
m: who said: Ibn Abi Jaʿfar narrated to us, on the authority of his father, on the authority of al-Rabiʿ: But
h
so that my heart may be reassured
. He said: Ibrahim wanted to increase his certainty.

c: Al-Muthanna told me, he said, Muhammad bin Katheer Al-Basri told us, he said, Israel told us, he said, Abu Al-Haitham told us, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubair:
m: h
So that my heart may be reassured
, he said: So that my certainty may increase.

c: Al-Muthanna told me, he said, Al-Fadl bin Dukayn told us, he said, Sufyan told us, on the authority of Abu Al-Haitham, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubair:
m: But
h
so that my heart may be reassured
, he said: so that my certainty may increase.

c: Saleh bin Mismar told us, he said, Zaid bin Al-Habbab told us, he said, Khalaf bin Khalifa told us, he said, Laith bin Abi Salim told us, on the authority of Mujahid and Ibrahim,
m: regarding his statement:
h
So that my heart may be reassured
, he said: So that I may increase in faith along with my faith.

c: Saleh told us, Zaid told us, Ziyad told us, on the authority of Abdullah Al-Amiri, who said, Laith told us, on the authority of Abu Al-Haitham, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubair,
m: regarding God’s statement:
h
So that my heart may be reassured
, he said: So that I may increase in faith along with my faith. We have previously mentioned the statement of someone who said that the meaning of his saying,
h
So that my heart may be reassured
, is that I am your friend.

x: Others said that the meaning of his saying,
h
So that my heart may be reassured
, is that I know that you will answer me if I call upon you, and give me if I ask you.
Who said that?

c: Al-Muthanna told me, he said, Abdullah bin Saleh told us, he said, Muawiyah told me, on the authority of Ali, on the authority of Ibn Abbas,
m: regarding his statement:
h
So that my heart may be reassured

, he said: I know that you will answer me when I call upon you, and give me when I ask you. As for the interpretation of his saying: He said, ‘Have you not believed?’, it is: Have you not believed? Like: Musa told me, he said, Amr told us, he said, Asbat told us, on the authority of Al-Suddi.

c: Ahmad bin Ishaq told us, Abu Ahmad told us, Sufyan told us, on the authority of Qais bin Muslim, on the authority of Saeed bin Jubair,
m: regarding his statement: Have you not believed? He said: Have you not been certain that I am your friend?

c: Yunus told me, he said, Ibn Wahb told us, he said, Ibn Zayd said
m: regarding his statement: Have you not believed? He said: Have you not been certain?

x: God Almighty meant by that: God said to him: Then take four birds, and he mentioned that the Surat Al-Baqarah 2:260
h
And when Abraham said

, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." He said, "Do you not believe?" He said, "Yes, but [it is] to reassure my heart." He said, "Then take four birds and bring them close to you, then place a portion of them on every mountain, then call them, they will come to you running. And know that God is Exalted in Might and Wise." four birds were: the rooster, the peacock, the raven, and the pigeon.
Who said that?

c: Ibn Hamid told us, Salamah told us, Muhammad ibn Ishaq told me, on the authority of some scholars:
m: The people of the first book mention that he took a peacock, a rooster, a crow, and a pigeon.

c: Al-Muthanna told me, he said, Abu Hudhayfah told us, he said, Shabl told us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid, he said:
m: The four birds are: the rooster, the peacock, the crow, and the pigeon.

c: Al-Qasim told us, Al-Hussein told us, Hajjaj told me:
m: He said, ‘The thigh of four birds.’ Ibn Jurayj said: They claimed that it was a rooster, a crow, a peacock, and a pigeon.

c: Yunus told me, he said, Ibn Wahb told us, he said, Ibn Zayd said:
m: He said, ‘Take four birds.’ He said: So he took a peacock, a pigeon, a crow, and a rooster, different in their species and colors.

x: There are different readings of this. The majority of the people of Medina, Hijaz and Basra read it as: Fasarahunna ilayka with a damma on the sad, from the saying of the speaker: I turned to this matter if I inclined towards it, I draw pictures. And it is said: I am towards you to draw pictures, meaning: I am yearning and inclined.

i: And from this is the saying of the poet:
x: God knows that we are looking forward to our neighbors on the day of separation.

It is the plural of asour, soura’, and soor, like aswad, souda’, and sowad. From this comes the saying of al-Tirmaah: Chaste except for that, or that he portrays her as passion, and passion is a stroke for lovers He means by his saying: Or that his desires may shape it, and incline it. The meaning of his saying: So turn them to you is to bring them close to you and face them towards you, as one says: Turn your face to me, meaning, turn them towards me. And from the aspect of his saying: So turn them to you to this interpretation, there was in the speech, according to him, something that he had left out, which he had left out, sufficing with the apparent meaning of it.

i: And its meaning then, according to him, would be: “He said:
x: Take four birds and turn them to you,” then he cut them up, then place a part of them on each mountain. It may be possible that the meaning of this, if it is read in this way with a dammah on the sad, is: to cut them off, as Tobah bin Al-Humayr said: When I pulled the rope, its webs creaked with the ends of the sticks, the walls of which were very strong. So the reasons brought me closer until I reached it with my rise, and my ascent almost depicted it.
Meaning: cut it. If this is the interpretation of his saying:
h
Then bring them to you
, then there is an inversion in the speech, and its meaning would be: Take four of the birds to you and bring them to you, and to you would be a connection to take.
A group of people from Kufa read it as Fasrahenu ilayk with a kasra, meaning: cut them off.

A group of Kufan grammarians claimed that they did not know fasrahinna or fasrahinna to mean cut them off in the speech of the Arabs - and that they did not know the kasra of the sad and its damma in that except with one meaning, and that they are both languages with the meaning of inclination, and that the kasra of the sad among them is a language of Hudhayl and Sulaym, and they recited for some of the Banu Sulaym: A branch that becomes good and is preserved as if it were on the light of the vineyards He means by his saying: becomes, inclines, and that the people of this language say: He made him become, and he makes him become becoming, and make your face towards me, meaning make it inclined, just as you say: make it inclined. Some grammarians of Kufa claimed that he did not know of any reason for the statement: Fasrahenna, nor for the reading of those who read Fasrahenna with a damma or kasra on the sad, for the cutting, except that it is: Fasrahenna ilayka! in the reading of those who read it with a kasra on the sad from the reversed.

That is because the lam of his verb was made in place of its ‘ayn, and its ‘ayn in place of its lam. So it would be from: sara yasri sariyan, for the Arabs say: he spent the night yasri fi hudhu, if he drew water, then he cut and drew water.

i: And from that is the saying of the poet:
x: I became a look, if I came across a walnut shield tomorrow and the storms were wailing from the blood of the hollow I became, I took a look, and from it the other said: They say: Syria kills its people! Who will I have if I do not bring it immortality!! My fathers, why don't you save them from death if they don't go, and my grandfathers!?

Meaning: He cut them off, then its ya’, which is the lam of the verb, was moved and made the ‘ayn of the verb, and its ‘ayn was changed and made its lam, so it was said: sara yasir, just as it was said: ‘atha ya’tha ‘athan, then its lam was changed and made its ‘ayn, so it was said: ‘ath ya’ith. As for the grammarians of Basra, they said: Fasrahenna ilayk has the same meaning if it is read with the damma of the sad and with the kasra, in that it means in this place: cutting. They said: They are two dialects: one of them is: sara yasawur, and the other is: sara yasir, and they cited as evidence for that the verse of Tawbah ibn al-Humayr that we mentioned before, and the verse of al-Mu’alla ibn Jamal al-Abdi. And the robe of the trampling of Safaya came, depicting her neck as a dark-skinned bastard Meaning: He splits her neck and cuts it, and in the verse of Khansa: The smell of it remained as it was It means by al-Shams 91:the mountains, that they crack and disperse - and in the verse of Abu Dhu’ayb: So help those who are frightened and block their paths against the predators: loyal and generous They said: The saying of the speaker: I became the thing, has two meanings: I dictated it, and I cut it off.
And they narrated a hearing: We became the judge with it, we separated the judgement with it.

This statement which we have mentioned from the Basrans: that the meaning of the damma in the Ṣād in His statement: Fasrīhinā ilayk and the kasra, are the same in meaning - and that they are two dialects, their meaning in this case: So cut them off - and that the meaning of ilāyk is to bring it forward before Fasrīhinā because it is the connection to His statement Fakḥ- is more correct than the statement of those grammarians of Kufa whose statement we have mentioned, who denied that there is any meaning for cutting in that except in the meaning of the heart which I have mentioned - due to the consensus of the people of interpretation that the meaning of His statement:
h
Fasrīhinā does not come out of one of two meanings

: either cut them off, or join them to you, with the kasra it was read that way or with the damma. So in the consensus of all of them on that, without their taking into account the kasra and damma of the Ṣād, nor their differentiation between the meaning of the two readings, I mean the kasra and the damma, the clearest evidence for the correctness of the statement of the grammarians of Basra who said that which we have mentioned from their statement, and the error of the statement of the grammarians of Kufa.

Because if they had interpreted his saying: Fasarihinna to mean He cut them off, on the basis that the original sentence was Fasarihinna, then it was reversed and it was said: Fasarihinna with a kasra on the sad, because the ya was changed, Fasarihinna was replaced by the ra, and the ra was transferred to the ya, then there would have been no doubt - with their knowledge of their language and their awareness of their logic - that they would have separated between the meaning of that when it was read with a kasra on the sad, and between it when it was read with a damma on the sad. Since it would not have been permissible for someone who reversed Fasarihinna to Fasarihinna to read it Fasarihinna with a damma on the sad. And despite the difference in their reading of that, they interpreted it with one interpretation in one of the two ways that we mentioned, so in that is the clearest evidence of the error of the one who said that that when it was read with a kasra on the sad it is interpreted as: cutting, reversed from Sari yasra to Sara yasir.

And the one who claimed that the saying of the speaker Asara yasura and Sara yasir is not known in the speech of the Arabs to mean: cutting off is ignorant. Those who were present mentioned that his interpretation of the words of God Almighty: So he cut them off means: So he cut them off.

c: Sulayman ibn Abd al-Jabbar told us, he said: Muhammad ibn al-Salt told us, he said: Abu Kudayna told us, on the authority of Ata’, on the authority of Sa’id ibn Jubayr, on the authority of Ibn Abbas:
m: So he split them, he said: It is Nabataean, so he split them.

c: Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna told us, Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar told us, Shuʿbah told us, on the authority of Abu Jamrah, on the authority of Ibn ʿAbbas, that he said
m: about this verse: Then take four birds and drive them to you, he said: It is only a parable. He said: Cut them up, then place them in the four quarters of the world, a quarter here and a quarter there, then call them and they will come to you running.

c: Al-Muthanna told me, he said, Abdullah bin Saleh told us, he said, Muawiyah told me, on the authority of Ali bin Abi Talha, on the authority of Ibn Abbas:
m: He cut them off, he said: He cut them off.

c: Yaqub told me, he said, Hisham told us, he said, Husayn told us, on the authority of Abu Malik,
m: regarding his statement:
h
Then cut them off to you
, he said: cut them off.

c: Al-Muthanna told me, he said, Amr bin Awn told us, he said, Hisham told us, on the authority of Hisin, on the authority of Abu Malik,
m: the same.

c: Abu Kuraib told us, he said, Yahya bin Yaman told us, on the authority of Ash’ath, on the authority of Ja’far, on the authority of Sa’id:
m: So make them sever, he said: He said: The wing of this is at the head of this, and the head of this is at the wing of this.

c: Muhammad bin Abdul A’la told us, he said, Al-Mu’tamir bin Sulayman told us, on the authority of his father, he said:
m: Abu Amr claimed, on the authority of Ikrimah, regarding his statement:
h
Then cut them to yourself
, he said, Ikrimah said: In Nabataean, he cut them.

c: Ahmad bin Ishaq told us, Abu Ahmad told us, Israel told us, on the authority of Yahya, on the authority of Mujahid:
m: h
Then cut them off to you
, he said: cut them off.

c: Al-Muthanna told me, he said, Abu Hudhayfah told us, he said, Shibl told us, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid:
m: h
Then bring them to you
, pluck them with their feathers and their meat, tearing them apart, then mix their meat with their feathers.

c: Muhammad bin Amr told me, he said, Abu Asim told us, on the authority of Isa, on the authority of Ibn Abi Nujayh, on the authority of Mujahid:
m: h
Then bring them to you
, he said: pluck them by their feathers and their flesh, tearing them apart. Surat Al-Baqarah 2:260
h
And when Abraham said

, "My Lord, show me how You give life to the dead." He said, "Do you not believe?" He said, "Yes, but [it is] to reassure my heart." He said, "Then take four birds and bring them close to you, then place a portion of them on every mountain, then call them, they will come to you running. And know that God is Exalted in Might and Wise."

c: Bishr bin Muadh told us, Yazid bin Zari’ told us, Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada:
m: h
Then bring them to you
, the Prophet of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, was commanded to take four birds and slaughter them, then mix their meat, feathers, and blood.

c: Al-Hasan bin Yahya told us, he said, Abd al-Razzaq told us, he said, Muammar told us, on the authority of Qatada,
m: regarding his statement:
h
Then tear them to pieces
. He said, Then mix blood with blood, and feathers with feathers. “Then place a portion of them on every mountain.”

c: It was narrated on the authority of Al-Husayn bin Al-Faraj
m: who said: I heard Abu Muadh who said: Ubayd bin Sulayman told us who said: I heard Al-Dahhak say: So turn them to you, meaning: So split them, and in Nabataean it is sara, which means splitting.

c: Musa told me, he said, Amr told us, he said, Asbat told us, on the authority of Al-Suddi:
m: So cut them to yourself, meaning cut them off.

c: It was narrated on the authority of Ammar,
m: who said: Ibn Abi Jaʿfar narrated to us, on the authority of his father, on the authority of al-Rabiʿ, regarding his statement:
h
Then bring them to you
, meaning: cut them to you and tear them apart.

c: Ibn Hamid told us, he said, Salamah told us, on the authority of Ibn Ishaq:
m: He cut them off means he cut them off. It is the image in the speech of the Arabs.

x: In what we have mentioned of the statements of those whose words we have narrated in the interpretation of His statement: So cut them to you, that it means: So cut them to you, there is clear evidence of the correctness of what we have said in that regard, and the corruption of the statement of those who disagreed with us in it. Since this is the case, whether the reader reads it with a damma on the sad: fasirhunna ilayk, or with a kasra on it fasirhunna, since they are two well-known languages with the same meaning. However, even if this is the case, what I prefer is to read it with it: fasirhunna ilayk, with a damma on the sad, because it is the higher and more famous of the two languages, and the most common among Arab tribes. [As for the statement of those who interpreted his statement: And turn them towards you to mean: gather them towards you, direct them towards you, and gather them, this is a statement that was made by a small number of the people of interpretation.]
Who said that?

c: Muhammad bin Saad told me, he said, my father told me, he said, my uncle told me, he said, my father told me, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ibn Abbas:
m: So tie them to you, tie them: tie them up.

c: Al-Qasim told us, Al-Hussein told us, Hajjaj told me, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, who said,
m: I said to Ata’ about his statement:
h
Then bring them to you
, he said: Bring them to you.

c: Yunus told me, he said, Ibn Wahb told us, he said, Ibn Zayd said:
m: h
Then bring them to you
, he said: Gather them.

x: The people of interpretation differed in the interpretation of his saying:
h
Then place on every mountain a portion of them
Some of them said: He means by that: for every quarter of the world, a part of them.
Who said that?

c: Al-Muthanna told me, he said, Muhammad ibn Jaʿfar told us, he said, Shuʿbah told us, on the authority of Abu Jamrah, on the authority of Ibn Abbas:
m: Then place a portion of them on every mountain, he said: Place them in the quarters of the world: a quarter here, a quarter here, a quarter here, a quarter here, a quarter here, Then call them, they will come to you running.

c: Muhammad bin Saad told me, he said, my father told me, he said, my uncle told me, he said, my father told me, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ibn Abbas:
m: Then place a portion of them on every mountain, he said: When he bound them, he slaughtered them, then he placed a portion of them on every mountain.

c: Bishr told us, Yazid told us, Saeed told us, on the authority of Qatada, who said:
m: The Prophet of God was commanded to take four birds and slaughter them, then mix their meat, feathers and blood, then divide them into four mountains. He told us that he drew shapes on their wings and held their heads in his hand, so that bone would go to bone, feather to feather, and piece to piece, and that was in the sight of the friend of God, Abraham, peace be upon him. Then he called them and they came to him running on their feet, and he threw each bird its head. This is a parable that God gave Abraham, saying: Just as He sent these birds from these four mountains, so God will send people on the Day of Resurrection from the four quarters of the earth and its regions. Narrated on the authority of Ammar, who said:

c: Ibn Abi Jaʿfar narrated to us, on the authority of his father, on the authority of Ar-Rabiʿ, who said:
m: He slaughtered them, then cut them up, then mixed their meat and feathers, then divided them into four parts, and placed a part on each mountain. So bone went to bone, feather to feather, and piece to piece, and that was under the sight of the friend of God, Abraham. Then he called them and they came to him running, saying: Strung on their legs. This is a parable that God showed Abraham, saying: Just as these birds were sent from these four mountains, so God will send people on the Day of Resurrection from the four quarters of the earth and its regions.

c: Ibn Humayd told us, Salamah told us, Ibn Ishaq told us, on the authority of some of the scholars:
m: The People of the Book mention that he took the four birds, then cut each bird into four parts, then he went to four mountains and placed a quarter of each bird on each mountain. So on each mountain there was a quarter of a peacock, a quarter of a rooster, a quarter of a crow, and a quarter of a pigeon. Then he called them and said: Come, by God’s permission, as you were. So each quarter of them jumped toward its companion until they gathered, and each bird was as it was before he cut it. Then they came running to him as God had said. And it was said: O Abraham, this is how God gathers His servants and brings the dead back to life for the Resurrection from the East and West of the Earth, its Levant and its Yemen! So God showed him the resurrection of the dead by His power until he knew that, meaning: what Nimrod said was a lie and falsehood.

c: Yunus told me, he said, Ibn Wahb told us, he said, Ibn Zayd said:
m: Then place a portion of them on each mountain. He said: So he took a peacock, a dove, a crow, and a rooster. Then he said: Divide them, put the head of each one and the jaws of another in another and the feet of another with him. So he cut them up and divided them into quarters on the mountains, then he called them and they came to him all together, and God said: Just as you called them and they came to you, just as you revived these after this, so also gather these - meaning the dead.

x: Others said: Rather, the meaning of this is: Then place on each of the mountains that were the birds and beasts that used to eat the flesh of the beast that Abraham saw dead. When Abraham saw it, he asked to show him how to revive it and all the other dead things. They said: There were seven mountains.
Who said that?

c: Al-Qasim narrated to us, Al-Husayn narrated to us, Hajjaj narrated to me, on the authority of Ibn Jurayj, who said:
m: When Abraham said what he said, when he saw the beast from which the birds and beasts scattered when he approached it, and he asked his Lord what he asked, He said: Take four of the birds - Ibn Jurayj said: So slaughter them - then mix their blood, feathers and flesh, then place a part of them on each mountain where you saw the birds and beasts go. He said: So he made them seven parts, and held their heads near him, then he called them by the permission of God, and he looked at every drop of blood flying to the other drop, and every feather flying to the other feather, and every limb and every bone flying one to the other from the tops of the mountains, until every corpse met one another in the sky, then they came running until they reached its head.

c: Musa told me, he said, Amr told us, he said, Asbat told us, on the authority of al-Suddi, he said:
